reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / Low's Clinical Autonomic Disorders
clinicalPearls: Characterised by sudden, sharply demarcated unilateral facial (and sometimes upper thoracic) flushing and sweating, typically provoked by heat, exercise, or emotion
The flushing side is the normal side; the contralateral side fails to flush and sweat because of sympathetic dysfunction
Reflects a lesion of the sympathetic vasomotor and sudomotor fibres, often at the preganglionic T2-T3 level
The demarcation line down the midline of the face is the striking diagnostic clue
Frequently idiopathic and benign, but may be associated with Horner syndrome or Adie tonic pupils, overlapping with Ross syndrome
Secondary causes include structural lesions of the brainstem, spinal cord, or paravertebral sympathetic chain from tumour, surgery, or trauma
Investigation is directed at excluding a structural sympathetic lesion when features are atypical or progressive
Management is largely reassurance for idiopathic cases, with treatment of any identified underlying cause
reference.pathophysiology: Harlequin syndrome results from a unilateral lesion of the sympathetic vasomotor and sudomotor pathways supplying the face, most often affecting the preganglionic fibres arising around the second and third thoracic segments. Loss of sympathetic outflow on the affected side prevents the normal flushing and sweating response to thermal, exertional, or emotional stimuli, so only the intact contralateral side reddens and perspires, producing the sharply demarcated 'harlequin' appearance. The lesion may be idiopathic, presumed to reflect a focal autonomic neuropathy, or secondary to structural compression or injury of the sympathetic pathway; associated pupillary or Horner findings indicate more extensive autonomic involvement.
additionalDifferentials: Structural brainstem or cervical sympathetic lesion
additionalInvestigations: Detailed autonomic and pupillary examination for Horner syndrome or a tonic pupil
Pharmacological pupil testing where anisocoria is present
MRI of the brain, cervical spine, and thorax to exclude a structural sympathetic lesion
Thermoregulatory sweat test to map the sudomotor deficit
Chest imaging to exclude an apical or mediastinal lesion
redFlags: Accompanying Horner syndrome with pain suggesting carotid dissection or an apical lung lesion
Onset after trauma or surgery with structural implications
Systemic features suggesting an underlying malignancy
reference.prognosis: Idiopathic Harlequin syndrome is benign and usually cosmetically rather than functionally troublesome, often remaining stable or fluctuating over time; the prognosis in secondary cases depends on the underlying structural cause.
pitfalls: Mistaking the flushing (normal) side for the abnormal side
Assuming the syndrome is always idiopathic and missing an underlying structural lesion
Overlooking associated Horner syndrome or tonic pupils that broaden the differential
Failing to image when the presentation is atypical or progressive
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Reassure and observe in idiopathic cases, which are benign and usually only cosmetically troublesome so require no specific treatment
Investigate for and treat any underlying structural cause such as a tumour or compressive lesion of the sympathetic pathway
Recognise and manage associated autonomic features including Horner syndrome, Adie tonic pupils, and Ross syndrome overlap
Reserve interventional sympathetic procedures such as contralateral sympathetic block or sympathectomy for genuinely distressing cases
Monitor for progression or new neurological and autonomic signs that may indicate an evolving structural lesion
Refer to neurology or an autonomic specialist for characterisation and follow-up
Escalate to further imaging if new deficits emerge suggesting a secondary cause
